conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery team doctor. I hear you’ve been having a burning pain in your upper abdomen that goes up into your chest and throat. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s like my whole esophagus is on fire. It started a few days ago and it’s getting worse. I’m scared it’s the same thing as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with that. Any vomiting, blood, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No black stools. I haven’t really eaten—just water. I didn’t vomit blood this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you kept your tube feeds running at home up until today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I kept them going. I only stopped when I left for the ER because I didn’t know if I should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll restart them here and keep a close eye on how you tolerate them. We’re going to check labs and get an abdominal X-ray to make sure there’s no blockage or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? It feels like something is burning through me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sensation can be intense even when it’s irritation from acid or bile reflux. We’ll treat the symptoms right away while we evaluate. We’ll start an IV acid-suppressing medicine and nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—just making sure you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we have that listed and we’ll avoid them. For pain we’ll use acetaminophen and, if needed, your prescribed oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV pantoprazole now. We’re also adding prochlorperazine as needed for nausea, and we’ll continue your erythromycin since it helps your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time the erythromycin helped, but why is this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your surgical history, you can be prone to reflux and irritation at the surgical connection sites. Sometimes inflammation flares up. We’ll also add a medication called cholestyramine to bind bile acids, which can contribute to burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cholestyramine—does that cause diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but more often it causes constipation or bloating. We’ll watch your bowel pattern and keep your stool softener on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern and no free air—so no sign of a blockage or perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is stuck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—nothing suggests an obstruction on that study. That supports reflux or inflammation as the cause of the burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The burning is still there, but the nausea is a little better. Am I allowed to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on your baseline stage 3 diet—soft foods—only as tolerated, and continue tube feeds. The goal is to keep nutrition steady without worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The burning comes in waves, especially when I lie flat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with reflux. Try to stay as upright as you can, especially after feeds or any oral intake. We can also raise the head of the bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my labs okay? I’m worried I’m bleeding again from an ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function and electrolytes look stable. Your hemoglobin is a bit low on one of the checks, but we’re not seeing signs of active bleeding like black stools or vomiting blood. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked the GI team to see you. They may recommend an upper endoscopy—an EGD—to look directly at the stomach and the surgical connections to see if there’s irritation or ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many procedures. Is an EGD risky for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally low risk. It’s done with sedation, and it lets us see if there are ulcers or inflammation and whether there’s any narrowing or angulation that could be worsening reflux. We’ll only proceed if it’s the best next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The cholestyramine tastes awful. Do I really need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not pleasant. If bile reflux is contributing, it can make a meaningful difference. Let’s try it consistently for now, and we’ll reassess based on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI evaluated you this morning. They recommend adding ranitidine at bedtime in addition to the pantoprazole and sucralfate, and they agree with doing an EGD to better characterize what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on three acid medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They work in different ways: pantoprazole strongly suppresses acid, ranitidine adds extra suppression overnight, and sucralfate coats irritated areas to protect them while they heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the EGD shows an ulcer, does that mean surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Many small ulcers and gastritis can be treated with medication and avoiding triggers. The EGD helps us tailor therapy and make sure there’s no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning the EGD for today. You’ll need to be NPO—nothing by mouth—for a period beforehand. We’ll coordinate tube feeds around the procedure timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated and comfortable. Most people don’t remember the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious. Can I take my lorazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’ll be getting sedation, we’ll have anesthesia and GI guide what’s safe. We can help with anxiety here, but we need to avoid stacking sedating medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EGD is completed. The anatomy looks consistent with your post-surgical state. There was an angulation between the stomach body and antrum, but the scope passed easily and there was no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked—then why does it burn so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw small clean-based ulcerations with some friability at the gastro-gastric anastomosis, and redness in the antrum consistent with gastritis. Those irritated areas can cause significant burning and reflux symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Clean-based means it’s not bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—clean-based ulcers are less likely to be actively bleeding. We’ll still treat them aggressively with acid suppression and protective medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning after the EGD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The burning is still there but not as sharp. I actually ate some of the soft diet without it coming right back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Since your oral intake is improving, we’ll start stepping your tube feeds back down toward your outpatient rate, while making sure you’re still meeting nutrition goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried if you lower the tube feeds I’ll get weak again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it gradually and only if you’re taking enough by mouth. The goal is to avoid overfilling your stomach and worsening reflux, while keeping your nutrition stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to stay upright even overnight? I can’t sleep sitting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You don’t have to sit straight up, but elevating the head of the bed and avoiding lying flat right after feeds can help. Even a wedge pillow or raising the bed can reduce reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re transitioning you from IV pantoprazole to oral pantoprazole twice a day. That higher dose is important for healing the gastritis and the small ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking it once a day at home. Twice a day is safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—twice daily is commonly used for more severe symptoms or ulcer healing. We’ll also keep ranitidine at bedtime and continue sucralfate four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the erythromycin? I’ve been on it a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing it because it helps with gastric dysmotility—your stomach emptying—and that can reduce reflux. We’ll have you keep taking it as prescribed unless your outpatient team changes it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain control? Are you needing much oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not much. Mostly Tylenol. I don’t want to get constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. Use oxycodone only if needed, and keep taking docusate to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you’re looking much more comfortable. Are you tolerating the stage 3 diet and your tube feeds at the outpatient rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I still get some burning, but it’s manageable. I’m eating more than I was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your exam is reassuring—your abdomen is soft and not tender, and your G-tube site looks clean and dry. If things stay stable, we’ll plan discharge home with your existing tube-feed services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over exactly what meds I’m leaving with? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Key changes: pantoprazole is now 40 mg by mouth twice daily. New: cholestyramine 4 grams twice daily and ranitidine liquid 150 mg at bedtime. Continue sucralfate four times daily, erythromycin every 6 hours, and your other home meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for chest pain or trouble breathing, vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness, any blood or black material in vomit or stool, fever over 101.5, or worsening pain—especially if it changes location or goes to your chest or back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the ulcers heal with this? I’m worried it’ll just keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ulcers we saw were small and clean-based, and your symptoms improved with the medication regimen—that’s a good sign. Healing can take time, so staying consistent with the acid suppression, sucralfate, and upright positioning is important. You already have follow-up scheduled with your surgeon, and we’ll keep that appointment.
